strengths: The concept of decoupling multi-modal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) into a hierarchical structure—Macro-Level CoT for high-level task planning and Micro-Level CoT for MDP-based subtask execution—is a sensible approach to address the token explosion and sequence length challenges of interleaved text-image generation.
The use of macro and micro attention masks to enforce locality and restrict sequence dependencies is a practical and well-motivated design to stabilize training and improve computational efficiency.
The proposed method is evaluated across a variety of text-to-image and image editing benchmarks (GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, KRIS, RISE) showing promising results compared to some baselines.
weaknesses: The manuscript is clearly an incomplete draft. The subtitle of the paper explicitly reads '[Version 0.2: For Nano-Banana Like Generation]', indicating that this is a preliminary working version not ready for peer review.

Crucial details regarding the methodology are missing. The reinforcement learning (RL) training phase with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is introduced as a major step, yet the text states: 'Further details on the reinforcement learning setup will be provided in a future version of this work' (Section 3.3) and 'We will release the details of Reinforcement Learning Framework in the future' (Section B.2). This omission makes the approach impossible to reproduce or properly evaluate.

The methodology section is misleading. Section 3.1 details Parallel Decomposition and Progressive Refinement as part of the proposed Macro-Level planning strategies. However, Section 6 (Limitations) reveals that these strategies are not yet implemented or stable: 'we are actively developing more advanced strategies ... namely the Parallel Decomposition Mechanism and Implicit Planning via Progressive Refinement'. An academic submission should only present methods that have been fully developed and evaluated.

The 'Nano-banana like Generation' task, despite being highlighted in the title, is poorly evaluated. Section 4.5 is extremely brief and only presents a qualitative figure (Figure 6) with no quantitative metrics or baseline comparisons on the mentioned 3K dataset.
There are several typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'Unifed' in the Section 2 heading, 'Macor attention mask' in the Figure S1 caption) which suggest a rushed and unpolished draft.

strengths: The proposed macro-micro hierarchical reasoning framework (Uni-CoT) is an interesting concept for managing computational complexity in multimodal chain-of-thought.
The macro and micro attention masking schemes are logical designs to enforce locality and reduce redundant token interactions in unified understanding-generation models.
weaknesses: The paper is clearly an unfinished draft. It explicitly states that key details of the methodology and experiments are missing: e.g., 'Further details on the reinforcement learning setup will be provided in a future version of this work' (Sec. 3.3), 'We will release the details of Reinforcement Learning Framework in the future' (Sec. B.2), and 'We will detail the data distribution in the future' (Sec. C).

There are critical copy-paste errors and discrepancies in the experimental tables. In Table 1, the proposed model 'Uni-CoT' is listed twice with different numbers. In Table 2, 'Uni-CoT' is duplicated as two identical rows.
The bibliography contains several duplicate references (e.g., [10] and [11] are the same paper; [38] and [39] are also identical).

The academic rigor and terminology are weak. The title includes '[Version 0.2: For Nano-Banana Like Generation]', which is highly non-standard for a peer-reviewed submission. Furthermore, claiming 'Google introduced Nano-Banana [44]' is inaccurate, as the citation points to a generic website (nanobanana.ai) without any clear association with Google research.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting and well-motivated framework (Uni-CoT) that integrates hierarchical Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning with unified multi-modal understanding and generation models.

The hierarchical design (Macro-Level CoT for global planning and Micro-Level CoT for subtask execution) is a logical approach to mitigate the high computational cost and sequence length of multi-modal generation reasoning.
The use of specialized attention masks (Macro and Micro Attention Masks) to restrict visibility and maintain locality is a technically sound design choice.
The model is evaluated across a wide range of benchmarks (GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, KRIS, and RISE) and demonstrates strong performance in multi-modal generation and editing tasks.
weaknesses: The manuscript is incomplete. In Section 3.3 under the Reinforcement Learning subsection, it explicitly states: 'Further details on the reinforcement learning setup will be provided in a future version of this work.' Similarly, in the Supplementary Material Section B.2, it says: 'We will release the details of Reinforcement Learning Framework in the future.' This is unacceptable for a final submission to a peer-reviewed AI conference.

The lack of details surrounding the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and RL training stages makes the work non-reproducible. It is unclear how the pairwise annotations were handled and how the visual preference learning was structurally optimized.
The title of the manuscript contains draft placeholders ('[Version 0.2: For Nano-Banana Like Generation]'), which indicates the submission is unpolished and was rushed into peer review.

The paper lacks comprehensive ablation studies to verify the individual benefits of its main components, such as the macro planning strategy vs. the micro self-reflection, and the specific impact of the attention masks on performance.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Multi-modal CoT reasoning is highly token-intensive due to the need to generate and understand intermediate visual states, leading to severe computational and optimization bottlenecks. This paper addresses this head-on.

Elegant and technically sound hierarchical design: The macro-micro decomposition, coupled with macro and micro attention masks, successfully reformulates multi-modal reasoning. Restricting micro-level self-reflection to a Markov Decision Process (MDP) elegantly reduces attention complexity from quadratic to near-linear.

Supervised learning with MDP auxiliary tasks: The proposed training paradigm stabilizes the optimization of interleaved text-image trajectories by introducing four structured auxiliary objectives (e.g., action generation, reward estimation), making multi-modal CoT training highly scalable.

Comprehensive and strong empirical results: The model achieves state-of-the-art results on both generation-focused (GenEval, WISE) and understanding-focused (Jigsaw-R1) benchmarks, outperforming strong open-source unified models.

Excellent generalizability: The authors demonstrate the robustness of the Uni-CoT framework by applying it to two separate state-of-the-art unified architectures (BAGEL and BLIP3o), both yielding consistent and substantial improvements.
weaknesses: While the proposed attention masking schemes mathematically reduce the attention complexity to nearly linear $O(T)$, the actual wall-clock inference time and GPU memory usage overhead from sequentially generating multiple intermediate visual latents (via VAE/diffusion experts) remains relatively high. A more detailed wall-clock execution analysis comparing Uni-CoT to standard multi-modal generation would be helpful.

The dataset curation pipeline heavily relies on proprietary commercial models (GPT-4o, Qwen-plus) to synthesize the macro planning paths, micro self-reflections, and evaluations, which presents reproducibility and dependency challenges on closed-source APIs.

On general understanding benchmarks (e.g., MME, MMMU, MathVista in Table 3), the performance improvements over the base model (BAGEL) are somewhat marginal. It would be beneficial to clearly discuss why the framework's benefits are heavily concentrated on structured visual reasoning (like Jigsaw-R1) and generation tasks, rather than general VQA.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and active bottleneck in multi-modal Chain-of-Thought (CoT): the extreme computational overhead of generating and encoding visual intermediate states.

The proposed macro-micro hierarchical CoT framework is conceptually sound and theoretically elegant, successfully reducing token interaction complexity from quadratic O(T^2) to linear O(T) using structured attention masks.

Uni-CoT is versatile and unified, demonstrating strong capabilities in both visual understanding (e.g., Jigsaw-R1, MathVista) and visual generation/editing (e.g., WISE, GenEval, KRIS, RISE) under a single architecture.

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning multiple benchmarks across generation, understanding, and editing, and shows substantial improvements over competitive baselines. The generalization to a different base model (BLIP3o) further confirms the robustness of the framework.
weaknesses: The wall-clock time and practical inference latency are not fully discussed. While token interaction complexity is reduced from quadratic to linear, the absolute overhead of autoregressively generating multiple high-resolution images (each taking ~4,000 tokens) still presents a massive latency bottleneck in practice.

The details of the MDP inference execution could be more explicit. Specifically, it is not completely clear how the termination threshold for the reward/evaluation score is determined during inference, and whether an auxiliary head or text-parsing is used to output the scalar score.

The curation of the 30K multi-modal CoT dataset relies heavily on proprietary models (GPT-4o, Qwen-plus). This makes the exact data pipeline hard to reproduce from scratch without substantial API budgets.
There are minor typos and formatting issues, such as missing citation years in the text (e.g., 'Lu et al.', 'Zhang et al.' on page 1) and 'UNIFED' instead of 'UNIFIED' in the Section 2 header.

strengths: Well-motivated and coherent framework: The paper targets an emerging and important research direction—unified multimodal Chain-of-Thought (for both generation and understanding) within a single system—and addresses the critical token-explosion bottleneck.

Rigorous design for complexity reduction: By formulating the micro-level self-reflection as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and introducing custom attention masks (macro and micro), the model effectively avoids attending to the entire historical sequence, reducing the computational complexity of multi-step multimodal CoT from quadratic to near-linear.

Diverse and comprehensive evaluations: The approach is tested on both vision-to-text (understanding) and text-to-vision (generation/editing) benchmarks (such as GenEval, WISE, MMBench, MathVista, Jigsaw-R1, KRIS, and RISE). The results consistently demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and strong structured reasoning capabilities.

Good generalization and ablation studies: The authors show that the Uni-CoT framework can be integrated into other unified architectures (e.g., BLIP3o based on Qwen2.5-VL) with notable performance boosts, proving the framework's versatility.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on complex, proprietary data curation: The proposed framework relies on a curated dataset of around 30K samples containing planning and self-reflection trajectories. Constructing this data requires extensive bootstrapping from advanced closed-source models (such as GPT-4o), which might limit its reproducibility or ease of adaptation for low-resource setups.

Marginal improvements on standard understanding benchmarks: As shown in Table 3, while the proposed method achieves massive improvements on structured reasoning benchmarks (such as Jigsaw-R1), the performance improvements on general benchmarks (MME, MMMU, MathVista) are relatively minor compared to the base BAGEL model, showing that the benefit of sequential/hierarchical CoT is somewhat localized to complex reasoning-heavy tasks.

Minor presentation details: Some figures and charts in the appendix and main text are highly detailed, but the text inside Figure 1 and Figure 2 is slightly small and dense, which may require zooming in to read comfortably.
